transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, hi, thank you for seeing me. I guess... well, what brings me in is that my head just feels completely foggy lately. It’s hard to explain, but it’s like I’m walking through mud mentally. I’m a personal care aide, so I’m in and out of clients' houses all day, and I’ve started making these little mistakes in my client notes. Usually, I'm very particular about my notes because the next shift really relies on them to know exactly how the day went, but I'll sit down to write and just completely blank on what happened an hour ago. Or I’ll get up to do something for a client, walk into their kitchen, and just stand there completely forgetting what I was even about to do. 

It’s incredibly frustrating because this really isn’t like me at all. I've always been the organized one, you know? I took some college classes back in the day and always kept on top of my schedule and my responsibilities, so to suddenly have this... this thick fog where I can't even hold onto a simple thought or finish a basic task without second-guessing myself, it’s just really throwing me off. I just keep trying to push through it, but the little mistakes keep happening, and I really can't afford to let my clients down since they rely on me for their daily care, so I figured I had to come in and talk to somebody about it before it gets worse.
How long have you been experiencing this foggy feeling?

Well, let me think... it’s been a little while now. I’d say this whole low, guilty, foggy feeling has been hanging over me for about a month. Maybe a little over a month? It started right around the time the weather started turning, I remember because I was helping Mrs. Higgins—she’s one of my Tuesday/Thursday clients, lovely lady, used to be a baker—and I was helping her get her winter coats out of the cedar closet. And I just remember feeling so incredibly drained that day, like every movement took ten times the effort it usually does. At first, I thought maybe I was just coming down with a cold or something, you know? You’re in and out of people’s houses, you pick up a bug, it happens. But the cold never came. Just this... this heaviness. 

And it hasn't let up since. Every single morning for the past four weeks, I wake up and it’s right there waiting for me. I’ll sit on the edge of the bed and just stare at the wall, feeling guilty because I know I need to get up and get to work, but my brain just feels like it's wrapped in cotton. I mean, a whole month of this is just exhausting. I keep looking back at my calendar, trying to pinpoint the exact day it started, but it’s all just sort of blurred together into this one long, dragging month of feeling completely out of it.
Have you been feeling sad or down most of the time since you started experiencing this foggy feeling?

Well, yeah, I guess I have. It's... it's hard to describe exactly, but lately I wake up with this heavy, empty feeling right in the middle of my chest. It's like, I can get up, I can put my scrubs on, I can drive to my clients' houses and go through the motions of my shift. I can even talk to them, you know, ask Mrs. Higgins about her baking days or chat with Mr. Davis about the weather, but inside? Inside I just feel completely sad and flat. It's like someone just turned the volume down on all my emotions, except for this one lingering sadness that just won't go away. 

I remember last Thursday, I was sitting in my car eating my lunch between clients—just a turkey sandwich, nothing special—and I just felt this overwhelming wave of... nothingness. Just this deep, quiet sadness. And it's not like me. I'm usually the guy humming along to the radio, making sure my clients are smiling before I leave. But now, it's just this constant, dull ache. I try to shake it off, I really do. I tell myself, "Come on, you've got people depending on you, you can't be moping around," but it's just there, every single day, right beneath the surface, making everything feel so incredibly hollow.
Do you find yourself enjoying things you used to like before this foggy feeling started?

Well, I mean... no, not really. I guess I just haven't had the energy to even try to enjoy much of anything. It's funny you ask that, because I was just thinking about my garden the other day. I usually love being out in the yard, especially this time of year when the weather starts to shift. I've got these tomato plants that I usually baby along, you know, checking the soil, making sure they're staked right, pruning the little suckers off the stems so they grow strong. It's always been my little escape after a long day of taking care of other people. I can just go out there, get my hands in the dirt, and kind of reset my brain. 

But lately? I just look out the kitchen window at them and I feel... nothing. I know they need watering, I know the weeds are starting to creep in around the edges of the raised beds, but I just can't bring myself to care. The thought of going out there and doing the work just feels so exhausting, and even if I did, I know I wouldn't get that same sense of satisfaction I usually do. It's the same with watching the football games on Sunday. Usually, I've got the snacks laid out, I'm texting my buddies about the plays, really getting into it. Last Sunday, I turned the game on, sat on the couch for maybe twenty minutes, and just turned it off. It just felt like noise. Everything just feels so flat, like the color has been drained out of all the things that used to make me happy. I just don't have the interest anymore, and it's really starting to bother me because those were the things that kept me grounded, you know?
Have you noticed any change in your weight since you started feeling this way?

Weight? No, I don't... I don't think so. I mean, my clothes still fit the same. I was actually just putting on my favorite pair of jeans the other morning—the dark blue ones I usually wear on Fridays when my schedule is a little lighter and I don't have to wear the scrubs all day—and they buttoned up just fine, no tighter or looser than usual. I guess I haven't really been paying that much attention to the scale, to be honest. Usually, I try to weigh myself every Sunday morning, just to keep an eye on things, you know? Being on my feet all day, lifting clients, helping them out of bed or into the shower, you have to stay somewhat in shape. If you let yourself go, it makes the job ten times harder, and my lower back already gives me enough trouble as it is. 

But these past few weeks, with this whole fog happening, I just haven't even bothered to pull the scale out from under the bathroom cabinet. I just don't care enough to check. I'm still eating, I guess. Like I said, I had that turkey sandwich the other day. I still make my dinner when I get home, even if it's just heating up a can of soup or making some toast because I'm too tired to actually cook. But my appetite hasn't really vanished, and I haven't found myself eating everything in sight either. It's just sort of... neutral. Like eating is just another chore I have to get through, along with everything else. So, yeah, no real change in my weight that I've noticed. I'm pretty sure I'm sitting right around the same 185 I've been at for the last couple of years.
Have you been having any trouble sleeping since this foggy feeling started?

Yeah, actually, my sleep has been just... all over the place lately. It's really frustrating. Normally, after a long day of lifting clients and being on my feet, I hit the mattress and I'm out cold. I've always been a good sleeper. But now? I'll get into bed, turn off the lamp, and I just lie there staring at the ceiling. My brain just starts going, mostly thinking about family stuff, you know? Like my brother and the situation with my parents, or just random worries about my kids that normally wouldn't keep me up. But suddenly it's 1:30, then 2:00 in the morning, and I'm just analyzing every little detail of things I can't even control right now. I'll toss and turn, flip the pillow over to the cool side, try to get comfortable, but my mind is just stuck on all that family drama. 

And then, even if I do finally manage to drift off, it's not a restful sleep. I end up waking up way before my alarm even goes off. I have my phone set for 5:30 every morning so I have enough time to take a hot shower and make my coffee before I have to drive to my first shift, but lately my eyes will just pop open at 3:45 or 4:00 in the morning. And that's it. I'm just awake. I try to tell myself, "Come on, you have another hour and a half, just close your eyes, you need the rest," but I just can't really settle back down. I'll just lie there in the pitch black, listening to the house creak or the fridge humming in the kitchen, feeling completely exhausted but totally unable to drift off again. It just makes getting through the next day and doing my job feel even more like wading through wet cement, because I'm starting out running on empty.
Are there any activities that you still find pleasure in or look forward to?

I mean... honestly? No. I really can't think of a single thing. It's like I was saying before about the garden and the football games—it's just all gone. I used to look forward to Friday nights, too. Usually, my buddy Dave and I will go down to the local diner, grab a burger, maybe have a beer and just shoot the breeze for a couple of hours. It's been our routine for, I don't know, maybe five or six years now? Ever since our kids were in middle school together. We'd talk about work, complain about the cost of groceries, just normal stuff. It was a nice way to decompress after a long week of hauling clients around and dealing with all the physical strain of my job. 

But this past Friday, Dave texted me around 4:00, asking if we were still on, and I just stared at my phone for like ten minutes. The idea of going down there, sitting in a booth, trying to make conversation, pretending to be interested in whatever story he was telling about his boss... it just felt like climbing a mountain. I ended up telling him I had a headache and just stayed home. And the worst part is, I didn't even feel relieved when I canceled. I just felt empty. I just sat on the couch in the dark for a while. 

Even things with my kids—my daughter came over on Sunday. She usually comes by to do some laundry because her apartment building's machines are always broken, and normally I love having her around. We'll make some lunch, maybe watch a movie while her clothes are in the dryer. But this time, I just couldn't wait for her to leave. Not because I was mad at her or anything, but just because having to interact, having to smile and ask her about her classes... it took everything I had. I was just counting down the minutes until the dryer buzzed so she'd pack up her basket and go. So, yeah, no. There's really nothing I look forward to right now. It's just a matter of getting through the day, going through the motions, and waiting for it to be over, even though I know I won't sleep anyway. It's just this constant, heavy nothingness, no matter what I'm doing.
Have you had any thoughts of not wanting to be alive or wishing you could just disappear since you started feeling this way?

I mean... I wouldn't say I want to actually do something to myself. I'm not sitting here making a plan or figuring out how to, you know, end it. I could never do that to my kids, especially with everything else going on in the family right now. But... I won't lie, it has crossed my mind in a different way. 

Like, when I wake up at 3:45 in the morning and I'm just lying there in the dark, listening to the house settle, knowing I have another twelve-hour shift ahead of me where I have to pretend to be okay, lifting people, smiling, making small talk... sometimes I just think, man, it really wouldn't be the worst thing in the world if I just didn't wake up. If I could just stay asleep, permanently. Just... slip away quietly, you know? No more dragging myself through the mud, no more feeling this heavy, empty nothingness all day long. 

And honestly? That thought really scares me. It terrifies me, actually. Because I've never been that kind of person. Even when things got tough with the divorce a few years back, or when my dad got sick, I always kept pushing. I always wanted to be here. But lately, just the idea of not having to do this anymore... of not having to exist in this fog... it feels almost like a relief, just for a second, before the guilt kicks in. I'm not going to hurt myself, I promise I'm not. But just having those thoughts floating around in my head, creeping in when I'm exhausted and vulnerable... it's a really dark place to be, and I hate that my brain even goes there now.
Have you noticed yourself moving or speaking more slowly than usual since this foggy feeling started?

I don't... I don't think so. I mean, I know I said earlier that getting through the day feels like wading through wet cement, but that's more of an internal feeling, if that makes sense? Like, the effort it takes to do things is just massive right now, but my actual physical body... no, I don't think I'm actually moving in slow motion or talking any slower than I am right now. 

Just yesterday, for example, I was helping one of my regular clients, Mr. Henderson—he's an older guy, needs a lot of physical assistance getting from his bed to his wheelchair—and I was moving at my normal pace. Getting the gait belt on him, doing the pivot, getting him settled into the chair... it all happened on normal time. I really have to keep my pace up anyway because, well, as a personal care aide, our schedules are packed incredibly tight. You get maybe forty-five minutes, an hour tops per visit, and in that time you have to get them showered, dressed, their breakfast made, their morning pills sorted out... you really can't afford to move slow, or the whole day's schedule falls apart, you're late to the next house, and the agency gets on your case. So I'm still doing all the physical labor at my usual speed. I just have to really force myself to do it. 

And as for talking... no, I think I sound pretty much the same. My daughter didn't mention anything about me sounding weird or slow when she was over on Sunday, and believe me, she's the type who would immediately point it out if I was talking like a zombie or taking too long to answer her. It's really just the exhaustion and that heavy fog on the inside, but on the outside, I'm pretty sure I'm still moving and talking just like I always do.
Have you noticed any difference in how quickly or slowly you're reacting to things around you compared to how you used to be?

I mean, reacting to things... no, I wouldn't say there's a difference there either. It's kind of like what I was just saying about moving and talking. My reaction time seems totally fine, even if I feel like garbage on the inside. 

Like, take driving, for instance. I spend half my day in my car, driving from one client's house to the next. The agency covers this huge area, so I'm constantly on the road, taking the interstate, dealing with the crazy morning traffic, merging, all that stuff. And you really have to be on your toes, especially with the way people drive around here lately. Just the other day, maybe Tuesday? I was heading over to Mrs. Gable's house—she's out in the suburbs, usually takes me about twenty-five minutes to get there—and this guy in a silver Honda just completely cut me off. Didn't use his blinker, just swerved right into my lane because he was about to miss his exit. I had to slam on my brakes so hard my work bag went flying off the passenger seat onto the floorboard. My coffee almost spilled everywhere. But I reacted instantly, you know? My foot hit the brake before I even had time to really process what was happening. If my reactions were slowed down, I definitely would have rear-ended him, and then I would have had to deal with the police, insurance, the agency getting mad that I missed a shift... it would have been a whole nightmare. 

So, physically reacting to things, catching things if they fall, hitting the brakes... that's all still sharp. Even with the clients, if someone starts to lose their balance—which happens a lot, especially with the stroke patients—I'm right there, catching them, steadying them, just like I always have. It's just... it's just the mental part. It's the having to get up and do it, the having to care about doing it, that's where the problem is. But the actual physical wiring? The reflexes? No, I haven't noticed any delay with that at all. It's all still working the way it's supposed to, even if the rest of me feels like it's shutting down.
Have you noticed yourself fidgeting, pacing, or feeling an inability to sit still since this foggy feeling started?

No, actually... it's kind of the exact opposite. If anything, sitting still is pretty much all I want to do right now. I definitely don't have that restless energy, you know, where you feel like you have to jump out of your skin or pace holes in the carpet. 

Like, when I get home from my shift—usually around 6 or 6:30, depending on if my last client needs extra help getting settled for the evening—I just drop my work bag by the front door and collapse into the recliner in the living room. And I mean, I will sit there for hours. Just staring. Not even turning the TV on half the time. The other night, I think it was Thursday, I sat down and after about an hour I realized my foot had completely fallen asleep, just totally numb, but I didn't even want to shift my weight to wake it up. I just let it tingle because moving my leg just seemed like too much of a production. So no pacing, definitely no pacing. I don't have anywhere near the energy required to pace around the house.

And as far as fidgeting goes... my hands are usually just completely still, resting in my lap. I used to be a bit of a leg-bouncer, you know? Like when you're sitting in a waiting room or sitting at a red light, just tapping the heel of your foot. I think I picked that habit up back when I was taking a few classes at the community college years ago, just nervous energy before exams, and I've kind of always done it since. But now? Nothing. I can sit perfectly still for an uncomfortable amount of time. Sometimes my kids will come into the room and actually ask if I'm okay because I'm just sitting so quietly—not bouncing my leg, not playing with my phone, not tapping my fingers on the armrest like I normally do when I'm watching a basketball game. 

It's just... stillness. A really heavy, exhausting stillness. So, yeah, no restless pacing or fidgeting or anything like that. Once I sit down, I am pretty much anchored to whatever chair I fall into until I absolutely have to force myself back up.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight since this foggy feeling started?

No... no, I haven't lost any weight, not that I've noticed anyway. You'd think with how exhausting everything feels, maybe I wouldn't have the appetite to eat, but honestly, my weight has stayed pretty much exactly the same. 

My scrubs—I wear these navy blue scrubs for the agency, they're kind of a stiff cotton blend, so they're really not very forgiving if you gain or lose a lot of weight—they still fit exactly the way they did a few months ago. The waistband isn't loose or anything. And my eating habits haven't really changed all that much during the day. When you're driving from house to house all day like I do, you don't really have the time to sit down for a proper meal anyway. You just kind of eat when you can. I usually just hit the drive-thru at Wendy's, or maybe grab a turkey wrap from that little deli over on 4th Street if I happen to have a ten-minute window between my morning clients and my afternoon folks. I just eat right there in the car, resting the sandwich on the center console, trying not to get crumbs all over my uniform before I have to go help someone with their physical therapy exercises. 

And then when I get home... well, like I was saying earlier about just collapsing in the recliner, I definitely don't have the energy to stand at the stove and cook a whole meal from scratch. I mean, I used to make a pretty decent chicken stir-fry, or at least I'd brown some ground beef and boil some pasta, but lately? It's just whatever takes the absolute least amount of effort. I'll microwave one of those frozen Marie Callender's meals, or honestly, sometimes I just eat half a sleeve of Ritz crackers and a couple slices of cheddar cheese while I'm sitting there in the chair staring into space. So the calories are definitely still going in, you know? It might even be worse calories than normal because it's all just quick, easy convenience food that I don't have to think about. 

But yeah, I actually stepped on the scale in my bathroom maybe a week or so ago, just out of curiosity when I was getting out of the shower, and it was hovering right around my usual 185. It really hasn't budged a single pound in either direction. So, no, no significant weight loss at all.
Do you feel like you're moving more slowly than you used to, or that it's harder to initiate physical activity?

I mean... no, I wouldn't say I'm moving in slow motion or anything like that. And as far as actually starting a physical activity, like getting up to do a task? No, I just do it. I mean, with my job, you really can't afford to move slow or drag your feet. 

Take my morning client, Mr. Henderson, for example. I've been seeing him for about two years now, every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. He's a pretty big guy, probably around 220 pounds, and he's completely bedbound, so getting him up and ready for the day is a whole physical production. But I walk in there at 8 AM sharp, put my bag down, wash my hands at the kitchen sink—because his daughter is really particular about germs, which I totally get, you know, you can never be too careful—and I just get right to it. There's no hesitation or standing around trying to get my body to work. I just roll him over, get the Hoyer lift sling tucked under his back, hook up the chains, and pump the handle. 

And you have to move at a pretty good clip, too, because it's really uncomfortable for them to just be hanging there in the sling while you maneuver the machine. That carpet in his bedroom is this thick, awful shag from the seventies, so you really have to put your back into pushing the wheels to get him over to the commode. If I was moving slower than normal, or if I couldn't initiate the movements right away, it would take all morning just to get him into his wheelchair, and it would completely throw off my schedule. I usually have three more people to see before lunch, so I have to keep a steady pace. 

So physically? No. My body moves exactly the same way it always has, at the exact same speed. Like I was saying earlier, I might not have the mental drive to cook a meal when I get home, and I might just sit in my recliner because I'm mentally exhausted, but the actual physical mechanism of getting up and moving? It's totally fine. I might be forty-three and a little stiff in the knees when it rains, but I'm definitely not moving any slower than I used to, and I don't have any trouble physically starting a task once it's time to do it.
Do you feel like it takes you a lot of effort to start doing something, even if it's a small task?

Well, I guess... I mean, yes, in terms of the toll it takes on me, absolutely. Like I was just saying, I can physically get up and do the work, I don't have a problem getting the motor running, so to speak. But the sheer amount of energy it drains from me? It's ridiculous. 

It’s just this deep, heavy feeling in my bones. Even on my days off, like on a Sunday when I don't have any clients scheduled and I literally don't do much of anything besides sit in that recliner I told you about, my body just feels completely worn out. I'll wake up after sleeping all night and feel like I haven't rested for a single second. 

And those small tasks, like you asked about... yeah, they just take way more out of me than they should. Take helping a client with a shower, for instance. I have this one lady on my Tuesday/Thursday route, and getting her showered isn't even the hardest part of my week physically—she has a shower chair and can stand on her own for a few minutes while I wash her back—but by the time I'm done getting her dried off and dressed in her clean clothes, I feel like I just ran a marathon. I'm just totally depleted. 

Or even just my own errands, like carrying groceries into the house. I used to just loop all the plastic bags from Kroger over my arms, you know, try to do it all in one trip so I wouldn't have to walk back out to the driveway. Probably six or seven bags at a time, plus maybe a gallon of milk or a pack of Gatorade. But now? Just grabbing two or three bags and walking up the three steps to my front porch feels like this monumental effort. I get inside and I have to drop them on the kitchen table and just lean against the counter for a minute because it just takes so much out of me. 

So yeah, the effort required for just... just normal, everyday things, it's exhausting. I can start the task, sure, because I have to, but I'm just so tired all the time, even when I haven't really done anything to earn it.
Do you feel like your thoughts are moving slower than they used to?

No... no, I wouldn't say my thoughts are slow. I mean, I can still think through everything I need to do just fine. You really can't have a slow brain in this line of work, because you're constantly juggling a million little details for a bunch of different people. 

Like, I have this one client, Mrs. Gable, she's an afternoon visit, usually right around 2:00. She's got this incredibly complicated medication regimen. I'm not a nurse, obviously, I'm just an aide, so I can't actually administer the meds, but part of my care plan is to give her reminders and make sure the plastic pill organizer is right there in front of her on the tray table. She takes a water pill, a blood pressure pill, something for her cholesterol, and then these two different prescription eye drops that have to be spaced exactly five minutes apart. And while I'm keeping track of that five-minute timer in my head, I'm also usually trying to swap over her laundry from the washer to the dryer, because her machine is one of those ancient top-loaders that gets off-balance easily and starts banging around like crazy if you don't distribute the wet towels just right. 

So my brain is constantly going, you know? Tracking the time, remembering where she keeps her special unscented detergent, making sure she actually swallowed the pills with her water and didn't just tuck them into her cheek—because she does that sometimes, bless her heart, she tries to hide them. I have to stay sharp to catch that kind of stuff. 

So, no, my thoughts are definitely still moving at their normal speed. I'm processing everything just fine, running down my mental checklists while I'm driving, anticipating what the clients are going to need before they even ask for it. It's really just that heavy, drained feeling in my body that I was talking about before. Mentally, the gears are turning exactly as fast as they always have. I just don't always have the physical battery power to back it up, if that makes sense. But the thoughts themselves? No, I haven't noticed them slowing down at all.
Do you feel like it's harder to make decisions than it used to be?

Well, making decisions... I mean, it kind of ties into the whole reason I actually made the appointment to come in and see you today. It’s not necessarily that I sit there paralyzed unable to pick between option A or option B, but my head just feels incredibly foggy lately. Just this thick, frustrating fog. 

And because of it, I’m making all these little mistakes, which is really what brings me in. Like, I have to fill out these client notes at the end of every shift. We use this app on our phones now—they phased out the paper binders last year, which was a whole headache on its own trying to get the older aides to learn the software—but anyway, I have to document every single thing we did during the visit. And lately, I’m catching myself making these dumb little errors. I'll check the box saying I prepped a hot meal when it was just a cold sandwich, or I'll type in the wrong time for when a client took their afternoon vitals. 

And on top of that, I'm also just... forgetting what I was about to do. I’ll walk from the kitchen to the bedroom to grab a fresh incontinence pad or a washcloth, and I’ll get to the doorway and just stand there, completely blanking on why I even walked in there in the first place. I have to retrace my steps to remember. It’s so frustrating because that is just not like me at all. I've always prided myself on being sharp and on top of the details. So, yeah, when it comes to making decisions or just thinking clearly in general... it's just really clouded by this fog right now, and it's definitely starting to mess with my work.
Do you feel like you're having trouble speaking or finding the right words when you're talking to people?

No, I haven't really noticed any issues with speaking or finding the right words. I mean, I'm still talking just as much as I always do. My wife always jokes that I could talk the ear off a brass monkey, and I guess that hasn't changed. Even with the brain fog I was just telling you about, once I actually remember what I'm trying to say, the words themselves come out just fine. 

Like, when I'm at work, communication is such a huge part of the job. You have to constantly be talking to the clients, keeping them engaged, reassuring them, especially the ones who get a little confused or agitated, like Mr. Henderson on my Monday/Wednesday route. He gets really anxious around bath time, just hates the water, gets it in his head that it's going to be freezing cold even though I always test it on my wrist first like you'd do for a baby's bottle. So I have to keep up this steady stream of chatter, you know, talking about the weather, or asking him about his old days working at the auto plant, just to distract him and keep him calm while I get him washed up. 

And I haven't had any trouble doing that. I'm not stumbling over my words or forgetting what a towel is called or anything like that. The vocabulary is all still there, right where I left it. I can still explain things clearly to the clients' families when they call to check in, like telling Mrs. Gable's daughter exactly how much of her lunch she ate or explaining that we need to order more of the thickener powder for her drinks. 

So the talking part, the actual physical act of speaking and finding the right words to use... no, that's completely fine. It's just the memory part, the walking into a room and forgetting why I'm there, or that thick, foggy feeling when I'm trying to log my notes at the end of the day. But once the thought is actually in my head, I have no problem at all getting it out of my mouth.
Do you think your current condition is interfering with your daily life in a mild way or is it having a more significant impact?

I mean... I'd say it's mild. It's not like I'm totally incapable of functioning or in danger of losing my job or anything dramatic like that. I'm still getting up, going to work, getting the job done. But it's definitely a nuisance, you know? It's having an impact, just in these really specific, frustrating ways that force me to change how I do things. 

Like I was saying about the documentation on that new phone app... I've actually started having to ask some of my coworkers to double-check my client notes before I hit submit at the end of the shift. Usually, I'll try to catch Brenda—she works the route right next to mine on the east side of town, we usually cross paths around 4:30—and I'll just have her look over my screen. I'll say, "Hey Brenda, does this look right for Mr. Henderson?" because I just don't trust myself right now to not make one of those dumb little errors I mentioned earlier. And she's great about it, she really is, she doesn't mind at all. But it's embarrassing, frankly, having to get someone to proofread my work like I'm a trainee again when I've been doing this for years. 

And then at home, it's spilling over there, too. My wife has actually had to take over paying some of the bills and handling our scheduling. Usually, I'm the one who sits down at the kitchen island on Sunday mornings with a cup of coffee and pays the water bill, the electric, makes sure the credit card is paid off, all of that. I've always been the one to handle the budget. But lately, because I'm just not as reliable with the details right now with this fog in my head, I almost paid the auto insurance twice last month, and I completely forgot to schedule the HVAC guy to come look at our furnace for its annual tune-up. 

So she just stepped in and said, "Let me take this off your plate for a while." Which is incredibly sweet of her, and it takes the pressure off, but it just goes back to that feeling of not being quite myself. So, yeah, I'd call the interference mild. I'm still doing the heavy lifting of my life. I just need a little extra scaffolding right now, I guess you could say, from Brenda and my wife, just to make sure the little details don't slip through the cracks.
Do you feel like your current condition is interfering with your daily life to the point where you're having trouble fulfilling your responsibilities as a personal care aide?

Well, like I was just saying a minute ago, it really depends on how you define "trouble," you know? Because the actual hands-on care—getting the clients out of bed, getting them bathed, making sure they're eating—I'm still doing all of that just fine. But a huge part of my responsibilities as an aide, and they drill this into us during our annual compliance training every single October, is the documentation. "If it's not documented, it didn't happen," that's what my supervisor, Diane, always says. It's tied to Medicare billing and liability, so it's a massive responsibility. 

And because of this brain fog, I really am having trouble with that specific part of the job. Like I said, I've had to pull my coworker Brenda aside almost every single afternoon to double-check my client documentation before I submit it on the app. And it's not just a one-off thing anymore; it's become this whole embarrassing routine where I literally wait around in the parking lot for her to finish her route on the east side just so I can have a second pair of eyes on my screen. If I didn't have her doing that, I'd probably be getting written up by Diane by now for all the little detail errors I'd be making. So in that sense, yes, it's absolutely interfering with my ability to fulfill my responsibilities entirely on my own. 

And it really is the exact same story at home with my responsibilities as a husband. Like I mentioned about my wife taking over the bills and the scheduling—that used to be entirely my domain. I was always the one who kept the household running on time, making sure the water bill was mailed and the furnace guy was booked. But because I'm just not reliable with those details right now, she's had to shoulder all of that extra weight. So, I guess when you look at the big picture, even though I'm still showing up and doing the heavy lifting, I'm definitely having trouble fulfilling my full responsibilities both at work and at home without relying on other people to catch my mistakes.

Just this deep, quiet sadness. And it's not like me. I'm usually the guy humming along to the radio, making sure my clients are smiling before I leave. But now, it's just this constant, dull ache. I've got these tomato plants that I usually baby along, you know, checking the soil, making sure they're staked right, pruning the little suckers off the stems so they grow strong. It's always been my little escape after a long day of taking care of other people. I can just go out there, get my hands in the dirt, and kind of reset my brain.

The thought of going out there and doing the work just feels so exhausting, and even if I did, I know I wouldn't get that same sense of satisfaction I usually do. Last Sunday, I turned the game on, sat on the couch for maybe twenty minutes, and just turned it off. It just felt like noise. Everything just feels so flat, like the color has been drained out of all the things that used to make me happy. I just don't have the interest anymore, and it's really starting to bother me because those were the things that kept me grounded, you know?

doctor.question: Have you been having any trouble sleeping since this foggy feeling started?

target_item.name: Sleep_Disturbance

patient.answer:
Yeah, actually, my sleep has been just... all over the place lately. It's really frustrating. Normally, after a long day of lifting clients and being on my feet, I hit the mattress and I'm out cold. I've always been a good sleeper. But now? I'll get into bed, turn off the lamp, and I just lie there staring at the ceiling. My brain just starts going, mostly thinking about family stuff, you know? Like my brother and the situation with my parents, or just random worries about my kids that normally wouldn't keep me up. But suddenly it's 1:30, then 2:00 in the morning, and I'm just analyzing every little detail of things I can't even control right now. I'll toss and turn, flip the pillow over to the cool side, try to get comfortable, but my mind is just stuck on all that family drama. 

And then, even if I do finally manage to drift off, it's not a restful sleep. I end up waking up way before my alarm even goes off. I have my phone set for 5:30 every morning so I have enough time to take a hot shower and make my coffee before I have to drive to my first shift, but lately my eyes will just pop open at 3:45 or 4:00 in the morning. And that's it. I'm just awake. I try to tell myself, "Come on, you have another hour and a half, just close your eyes, you need the rest," but I just can't really settle back down. I'll just lie there in the pitch black, listening to the house creak or the fridge humming in the kitchen, feeling completely exhausted but totally unable to drift off again. It just makes getting through the next day and doing my job feel even more like wading through wet cement, because I'm starting out running on empty.

I mean... honestly? No. I really can't think of a single thing. It's like I was saying before about the garden and the football games—it's just all gone. I used to look forward to Friday nights, too. Usually, my buddy Dave and I will go down to the local diner, grab a burger, maybe have a beer and just shoot the breeze for a couple of hours. But this past Friday, Dave texted me around 4:00, asking if we were still on, and I just stared at my phone for like ten minutes. The idea of going down there, sitting in a booth, trying to make conversation, pretending to be interested in whatever story he was telling about his boss... it just felt like climbing a mountain. I ended up telling him I had a headache and just stayed home. And the worst part is, I didn't even feel relieved when I canceled. I just felt empty. I just sat on the couch in the dark for a while. 

Even things with my kids—my daughter came over on Sunday. She usually comes by to do some laundry because her apartment building's machines are always broken, and normally I love having her around. We'll make some lunch, maybe watch a movie while her clothes are in the dryer. But this time, I just couldn't wait for her to leave. Not because I was mad at her or anything, but just because having to interact, having to smile and ask her about her classes... it took everything I had. I was just counting down the minutes until the dryer buzzed so she'd pack up her basket and go. So, yeah, no. There's really nothing I look forward to right now. It's just a matter of getting through the day, going through the motions, and waiting for it to be over, even though I know I won't sleep anyway. It's just this constant, heavy nothingness, no matter what I'm doing.

I mean... I wouldn't say I want to actually do something to myself. I'm not sitting here making a plan or figuring out how to, you know, end it. I could never do that to my kids, especially with everything else going on in the family right now. But... I won't lie, it has crossed my mind in a different way. 

Like, when I wake up at 3:45 in the morning and I'm just lying there in the dark, listening to the house settle, knowing I have another twelve-hour shift ahead of me where I have to pretend to be okay, lifting people, smiling, making small talk... sometimes I just think, man, it really wouldn't be the worst thing in the world if I just didn't wake up. And honestly? That thought really scares me. It terrifies me, actually. Because I've never been that kind of person. Even when things got tough with the divorce a few years back, or when my dad got sick, I always kept pushing. I always wanted to be here. But lately, just the idea of not having to do this anymore... of not having to exist in this fog... it feels almost like a relief, just for a second, before the guilt kicks in. I'm not going to hurt myself, I promise I'm not. But just having those thoughts floating around in my head, creeping in when I'm exhausted and vulnerable... it's a really dark place to be, and I hate that my brain even goes there now.

My daughter didn't mention anything about me sounding weird or slow when she was over on Sunday, and believe me, she's the type who would immediately point it out if I was talking like a zombie or taking too long to answer her. It's really just the exhaustion and that heavy fog on the inside, but on the outside, I'm pretty sure I'm still moving and talking just like I always do.

I mean, reacting to things... no, I wouldn't say there's a difference there either. It's kind of like what I was just saying about moving and talking. My reaction time seems totally fine, even if I feel like garbage on the inside. 

Like, take driving, for instance. I spend half my day in my car, driving from one client's house to the next. The agency covers this huge area, so I'm constantly on the road, taking the interstate, dealing with the crazy morning traffic, merging, all that stuff. And you really have to be on your toes, especially with the way people drive around here lately. Just the other day, maybe Tuesday? I was heading over to Mrs. Gable's house—she's out in the suburbs, usually takes me about twenty-five minutes to get there—and this guy in a silver Honda just completely cut me off. Didn't use his blinker, just swerved right into my lane because he was about to miss his exit. I had to slam on my brakes so hard my work bag went flying off the passenger seat onto the floorboard. My coffee almost spilled everywhere. But I reacted instantly, you know? My foot hit the brake before I even had time to really process what was happening. If my reactions were slowed down, I definitely would have rear-ended him, and then I would have had to deal with the police, insurance, the agency getting mad that I missed a shift... it would have been a whole nightmare. 

So, physically reacting to things, catching things if they fall, hitting the brakes... that's all still sharp. Even with the clients, if someone starts to lose their balance—which happens a lot, especially with the stroke patients—I'm right there, catching them, steadying them, just like I always have. It's just... it's just the mental part. It's the having to get up and do it, the having to care about doing it, that's where the problem is. But the actual physical wiring? The reflexes? No, I haven't noticed any delay with that at all. It's all still working the way it's supposed to, even if the rest of me feels like it's shutting down.

The symptom profile does not contain a specific symptom for psychomotor agitation/retardation during the depressive phase.

patient.answer:
No, actually... it's kind of the exact opposite. If anything, sitting still is pretty much all I want to do right now. I definitely don't have that restless energy, you know, where you feel like you have to jump out of your skin or pace holes in the carpet. 

Like, when I get home from my shift—usually around 6 or 6:30, depending on if my last client needs extra help getting settled for the evening—I just drop my work bag by the front door and collapse into the recliner in the living room. And I mean, I will sit there for hours. Just staring. Not even turning the TV on half the time. The other night, I think it was Thursday, I sat down and after about an hour I realized my foot had completely fallen asleep, just totally numb, but I didn't even want to shift my weight to wake it up. I just let it tingle because moving my leg just seemed like too much of a production. So no pacing, definitely no pacing. I don't have anywhere near the energy required to pace around the house.

And as far as fidgeting goes... my hands are usually just completely still, resting in my lap. I used to be a bit of a leg-bouncer, you know? Like when you're sitting in a waiting room or sitting at a red light, just tapping the heel of your foot. I think I picked that habit up back when I was taking a few classes at the community college years ago, just nervous energy before exams, and I've kind of always done it since. But now? Nothing. I can sit perfectly still for an uncomfortable amount of time. Sometimes my kids will come into the room and actually ask if I'm okay because I'm just sitting so quietly—not bouncing my leg, not playing with my phone, not tapping my fingers on the armrest like I normally do when I'm watching a basketball game. 

It's just... stillness. A really heavy, exhausting stillness. So, yeah, no restless pacing or fidgeting or anything like that. Once I sit down, I am pretty much anchored to whatever chair I fall into until I absolutely have to force myself back up.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of significant weight loss
doctor.question: Have you lost a significant amount of weight since this foggy feeling started?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about weight loss, which is not covered in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No... no, I haven't lost any weight, not that I've noticed anyway. You'd think with how exhausting everything feels, maybe I wouldn't have the appetite to eat, but honestly, my weight has stayed pretty much exactly the same. 

My scrubs—I wear these navy blue scrubs for the agency, they're kind of a stiff cotton blend, so they're really not very forgiving if you gain or lose a lot of weight—they still fit exactly the way they did a few months ago. The waistband isn't loose or anything. And my eating habits haven't really changed all that much during the day. When you're driving from house to house all day like I do, you don't really have the time to sit down for a proper meal anyway. You just kind of eat when you can. I usually just hit the drive-thru at Wendy's, or maybe grab a turkey wrap from that little deli over on 4th Street if I happen to have a ten-minute window between my morning clients and my afternoon folks. I just eat right there in the car, resting the sandwich on the center console, trying not to get crumbs all over my uniform before I have to go help someone with their physical therapy exercises. 

And then when I get home... well, like I was saying earlier about just collapsing in the recliner, I definitely don't have the energy to stand at the stove and cook a whole meal from scratch. I mean, I used to make a pretty decent chicken stir-fry, or at least I'd brown some ground beef and boil some pasta, but lately? It's just whatever takes the absolute least amount of effort. I'll microwave one of those frozen Marie Callender's meals, or honestly, sometimes I just eat half a sleeve of Ritz crackers and a couple slices of cheddar cheese while I'm sitting there in the chair staring into space. So the calories are definitely still going in, you know? It might even be worse calories than normal because it's all just quick, easy convenience food that I don't have to think about. 

But yeah, I actually stepped on the scale in my bathroom maybe a week or so ago, just out of curiosity when I was getting out of the shower, and it was hovering right around my usual 185. It really hasn't budged a single pound in either direction. So, no, no significant weight loss at all.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor agitation or retardation
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're moving more slowly than you used to, or that it's harder to initiate physical activity?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about psychomotor retardation (moving more slowly or difficulty initiating physical activity), which is not included in the patient's symptom profile.

patient.answer:
I mean... no, I wouldn't say I'm moving in slow motion or anything like that. And as far as actually starting a physical activity, like getting up to do a task? No, I just do it. I mean, with my job, you really can't afford to move slow or drag your feet. 

Take my morning client, Mr. Henderson, for example. I've been seeing him for about two years now, every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. He's a pretty big guy, probably around 220 pounds, and he's completely bedbound, so getting him up and ready for the day is a whole physical production. But I walk in there at 8 AM sharp, put my bag down, wash my hands at the kitchen sink—because his daughter is really particular about germs, which I totally get, you know, you can never be too careful—and I just get right to it. There's no hesitation or standing around trying to get my body to work. I just roll him over, get the Hoyer lift sling tucked under his back, hook up the chains, and pump the handle. 

And you have to move at a pretty good clip, too, because it's really uncomfortable for them to just be hanging there in the sling while you maneuver the machine. That carpet in his bedroom is this thick, awful shag from the seventies, so you really have to put your back into pushing the wheels to get him over to the commode. If I was moving slower than normal, or if I couldn't initiate the movements right away, it would take all morning just to get him into his wheelchair, and it would completely throw off my schedule. I usually have three more people to see before lunch, so I have to keep a steady pace. 

So physically? No. My body moves exactly the same way it always has, at the exact same speed. Like I was saying earlier, I might not have the mental drive to cook a meal when I get home, and I might just sit in my recliner because I'm mentally exhausted, but the actual physical mechanism of getting up and moving? It's totally fine. I might be forty-three and a little stiff in the knees when it rains, but I'm definitely not moving any slower than I used to, and I don't have any trouble physically starting a task once it's time to do it.

patient.answer:
Well, I guess... I mean, yes, in terms of the toll it takes on me, absolutely. Like I was just saying, I can physically get up and do the work, I don't have a problem getting the motor running, so to speak. But the sheer amount of energy it drains from me? It's ridiculous. 

It’s just this deep, heavy feeling in my bones. Even on my days off, like on a Sunday when I don't have any clients scheduled and I literally don't do much of anything besides sit in that recliner I told you about, my body just feels completely worn out. I'll wake up after sleeping all night and feel like I haven't rested for a single second. 

And those small tasks, like you asked about... yeah, they just take way more out of me than they should. Take helping a client with a shower, for instance. I have this one lady on my Tuesday/Thursday route, and getting her showered isn't even the hardest part of my week physically—she has a shower chair and can stand on her own for a few minutes while I wash her back—but by the time I'm done getting her dried off and dressed in her clean clothes, I feel like I just ran a marathon. I'm just totally depleted. 

Or even just my own errands, like carrying groceries into the house. I used to just loop all the plastic bags from Kroger over my arms, you know, try to do it all in one trip so I wouldn't have to walk back out to the driveway. Probably six or seven bags at a time, plus maybe a gallon of milk or a pack of Gatorade. But now? Just grabbing two or three bags and walking up the three steps to my front porch feels like this monumental effort. I get inside and I have to drop them on the kitchen table and just lean against the counter for a minute because it just takes so much out of me. 

So yeah, the effort required for just... just normal, everyday things, it's exhausting. I can start the task, sure, because I have to, but I'm just so tired all the time, even when I haven't really done anything to earn it.

doctor.question: Do you feel like your thoughts are moving slower than they used to?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about slowed thinking, which is a symptom of psychomotor retardation. This is not covered by the patient's symptom profile, which includes diminished ability to think or concentrate (S031) but not specifically psychomotor retardation.

patient.answer:
No... no, I wouldn't say my thoughts are slow. I mean, I can still think through everything I need to do just fine. You really can't have a slow brain in this line of work, because you're constantly juggling a million little details for a bunch of different people. 

Like, I have this one client, Mrs. Gable, she's an afternoon visit, usually right around 2:00. She's got this incredibly complicated medication regimen. I'm not a nurse, obviously, I'm just an aide, so I can't actually administer the meds, but part of my care plan is to give her reminders and make sure the plastic pill organizer is right there in front of her on the tray table. She takes a water pill, a blood pressure pill, something for her cholesterol, and then these two different prescription eye drops that have to be spaced exactly five minutes apart. And while I'm keeping track of that five-minute timer in my head, I'm also usually trying to swap over her laundry from the washer to the dryer, because her machine is one of those ancient top-loaders that gets off-balance easily and starts banging around like crazy if you don't distribute the wet towels just right. 

So my brain is constantly going, you know? Tracking the time, remembering where she keeps her special unscented detergent, making sure she actually swallowed the pills with her water and didn't just tuck them into her cheek—because she does that sometimes, bless her heart, she tries to hide them. I have to stay sharp to catch that kind of stuff. 

So, no, my thoughts are definitely still moving at their normal speed. I'm processing everything just fine, running down my mental checklists while I'm driving, anticipating what the clients are going to need before they even ask for it. It's really just that heavy, drained feeling in my body that I was talking about before. Mentally, the gears are turning exactly as fast as they always have. I just don't always have the physical battery power to back it up, if that makes sense. But the thoughts themselves? No, I haven't noticed them slowing down at all.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor retardation
doctor.question: Do you feel like it's harder to make decisions than it used to be?

target_item.name: Diminished_Thinking
target_item.manifestation: What brings me in is that my head feels foggy, and I’m making little mistakes in my client notes and forgetting what I was about to do, which isn’t like me.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question about whether it is harder to make decisions directly addresses the 'indecisiveness' aspect of the Diminished Thinking symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, making decisions... I mean, it kind of ties into the whole reason I actually made the appointment to come in and see you today. It’s not necessarily that I sit there paralyzed unable to pick between option A or option B, but my head just feels incredibly foggy lately. Just this thick, frustrating fog. 

And because of it, I’m making all these little mistakes, which is really what brings me in. Like, I have to fill out these client notes at the end of every shift. We use this app on our phones now—they phased out the paper binders last year, which was a whole headache on its own trying to get the older aides to learn the software—but anyway, I have to document every single thing we did during the visit. And lately, I’m catching myself making these dumb little errors. I'll check the box saying I prepped a hot meal when it was just a cold sandwich, or I'll type in the wrong time for when a client took their afternoon vitals. 

And on top of that, I'm also just... forgetting what I was about to do. I’ll walk from the kitchen to the bedroom to grab a fresh incontinence pad or a washcloth, and I’ll get to the doorway and just stand there, completely blanking on why I even walked in there in the first place. I have to retrace my steps to remember. It’s so frustrating because that is just not like me at all. I've always prided myself on being sharp and on top of the details. So, yeah, when it comes to making decisions or just thinking clearly in general... it's just really clouded by this fog right now, and it's definitely starting to mess with my work.

doctor.intent: Determine the presence of psychomotor retardation
doctor.question: Do you feel like you're having trouble speaking or finding the right words when you're talking to people?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about difficulty speaking or finding words, which relates to speech-related cognitive issues or psychomotor retardation. This specific symptom is not covered by the items in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
No, I haven't really noticed any issues with speaking or finding the right words. I mean, I'm still talking just as much as I always do. My wife always jokes that I could talk the ear off a brass monkey, and I guess that hasn't changed. Even with the brain fog I was just telling you about, once I actually remember what I'm trying to say, the words themselves come out just fine. 

Like, when I'm at work, communication is such a huge part of the job. You have to constantly be talking to the clients, keeping them engaged, reassuring them, especially the ones who get a little confused or agitated, like Mr. Henderson on my Monday/Wednesday route. He gets really anxious around bath time, just hates the water, gets it in his head that it's going to be freezing cold even though I always test it on my wrist first like you'd do for a baby's bottle. So I have to keep up this steady stream of chatter, you know, talking about the weather, or asking him about his old days working at the auto plant, just to distract him and keep him calm while I get him washed up. 

And I haven't had any trouble doing that. I'm not stumbling over my words or forgetting what a towel is called or anything like that. The vocabulary is all still there, right where I left it. I can still explain things clearly to the clients' families when they call to check in, like telling Mrs. Gable's daughter exactly how much of her lunch she ate or explaining that we need to order more of the thickener powder for her drinks. 

So the talking part, the actual physical act of speaking and finding the right words to use... no, that's completely fine. It's just the memory part, the walking into a room and forgetting why I'm there, or that thick, foggy feeling when I'm trying to log my notes at the end of the day. But once the thought is actually in my head, I have no problem at all getting it out of my mouth.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's condition is more aligned with F32.0 (Mild depressive episode) or F32.1 (Moderate depressive episode) based on the presence of marked psychomotor agitation or retardation
doctor.question: Do you think your current condition is interfering with your daily life in a mild way or is it having a more significant impact?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: At work I’ve had to ask coworkers to double-check my client documentation, and at home my wife has taken over some bills and scheduling because I’m not as reliable with details right now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the impact of my condition on my daily life, which corresponds to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
I mean... I'd say it's mild. It's not like I'm totally incapable of functioning or in danger of losing my job or anything dramatic like that. I'm still getting up, going to work, getting the job done. But it's definitely a nuisance, you know? It's having an impact, just in these really specific, frustrating ways that force me to change how I do things. 

Like I was saying about the documentation on that new phone app... I've actually started having to ask some of my coworkers to double-check my client notes before I hit submit at the end of the shift. Usually, I'll try to catch Brenda—she works the route right next to mine on the east side of town, we usually cross paths around 4:30—and I'll just have her look over my screen. I'll say, "Hey Brenda, does this look right for Mr. Henderson?" because I just don't trust myself right now to not make one of those dumb little errors I mentioned earlier. And she's great about it, she really is, she doesn't mind at all. But it's embarrassing, frankly, having to get someone to proofread my work like I'm a trainee again when I've been doing this for years. 

And then at home, it's spilling over there, too. My wife has actually had to take over paying some of the bills and handling our scheduling. Usually, I'm the one who sits down at the kitchen island on Sunday mornings with a cup of coffee and pays the water bill, the electric, makes sure the credit card is paid off, all of that. I've always been the one to handle the budget. But lately, because I'm just not as reliable with the details right now with this fog in my head, I almost paid the auto insurance twice last month, and I completely forgot to schedule the HVAC guy to come look at our furnace for its annual tune-up. 

So she just stepped in and said, "Let me take this off your plate for a while." Which is incredibly sweet of her, and it takes the pressure off, but it just goes back to that feeling of not being quite myself. So, yeah, I'd call the interference mild. I'm still doing the heavy lifting of my life. I just need a little extra scaffolding right now, I guess you could say, from Brenda and my wife, just to make sure the little details don't slip through the cracks.

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of the patient's condition
doctor.question: Do you feel like your current condition is interfering with your daily life to the point where you're having trouble fulfilling your responsibilities as a personal care aide?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: At work I’ve had to ask coworkers to double-check my client documentation, and at home my wife has taken over some bills and scheduling because I’m not as reliable with details right now.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the extent to which the patient's condition is interfering with his responsibilities at work, which directly relates to functional impairment.

patient.answer:
Well, like I was just saying a minute ago, it really depends on how you define "trouble," you know? Because the actual hands-on care—getting the clients out of bed, getting them bathed, making sure they're eating—I'm still doing all of that just fine. But a huge part of my responsibilities as an aide, and they drill this into us during our annual compliance training every single October, is the documentation. "If it's not documented, it didn't happen," that's what my supervisor, Diane, always says. It's tied to Medicare billing and liability, so it's a massive responsibility. 

And because of this brain fog, I really am having trouble with that specific part of the job. Like I said, I've had to pull my coworker Brenda aside almost every single afternoon to double-check my client documentation before I submit it on the app. And it's not just a one-off thing anymore; it's become this whole embarrassing routine where I literally wait around in the parking lot for her to finish her route on the east side just so I can have a second pair of eyes on my screen. If I didn't have her doing that, I'd probably be getting written up by Diane by now for all the little detail errors I'd be making. So in that sense, yes, it's absolutely interfering with my ability to fulfill my responsibilities entirely on my own. 

And it really is the exact same story at home with my responsibilities as a husband. Like I mentioned about my wife taking over the bills and the scheduling—that used to be entirely my domain. I was always the one who kept the household running on time, making sure the water bill was mailed and the furnace guy was booked. But because I'm just not reliable with those details right now, she's had to shoulder all of that extra weight. So, I guess when you look at the big picture, even though I'm still showing up and doing the heavy lifting, I'm definitely having trouble fulfilling my full responsibilities both at work and at home without relying on other people to catch my mistakes.
